To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the plasma cholesterol levels of patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) are significantly higher during hospitalization than at baseline, and the levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides are significantly higher than at baseline.

1) the plasma cholesterol level is not a risk factor for acute coronary events, and 2) the plasma cholesterol concentration does not increase after hospitalization for an acute coronary event, and may even decrease in some cases.
the cholesterol levels of patients hospitalized for acute coronary events were significantly lower than their prehospital levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the relationship of plasma cholesterol levels with the incidence of acute coronary events.
the effects of hospitalization on plasma lipoprotein levels in patients with acute coronary events.
the effects of hospitalization on plasma cholesterol levels in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) or unstable angina (UA).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cholesterol level is a risk factor for coronary heart disease and that lowering cholesterol levels by diet or drugs reduces that risk.
the cholesterol level of a person who has had a coronary event is not a useful predictor for future coronary events.
the changes in the plasma lipid levels after hospitalization of an acute coronary event are small and not clinically relevant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no clear evidence that cholesterol levels change after an acute coronary event.
the plasma cholesterol levels of the patients who had an acute coronary event and were hospitalized for the event, increased significantly after discharge from the hospital.
there are no changes in total cholesterol and LDL-cholesterol after acute coronary events and that HDL-cholesterol increases.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cholesterol levels of hospitalized patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) are lower than those of patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) who were not hospitalized, and that the cholesterol levels in both groups are significantly lower than those of healthy subjects.

the risk of a recurrent event in patients who have survived an acute coronary event (myocardial infarction, unstable angina, or sudden cardiac death) is strongly influenced by the plasma cholesterol concentration at the time of hospital discharge.

cholesterol levels in the blood can be used to predict the likelihood of a heart attack, and that cholesterol levels in patients hospitalized for heart attacks can be lowered with the right treatment.
